title: Leibniz
orientation: Russell presents Leibniz (1646-1716) as one of the supreme intellects of all time but not an admirable human being, arguing there were 'two Leibnizes': a popular, optimistic, published philosophy designed to please princes, and a profound, largely unpublished 'esoteric' system, more Spinozistic and rigorously logical, that Leibniz suppressed after Arnauld found it shocking. The chapter covers his life, his monadology, his four arguments for God's existence, his theory of the best of all possible worlds, and finally his private logical metaphysics based on subject-predicate logic.
historical_background: Leibniz was born near the end of the Thirty Years' War, studied law, worked for the Archbishop of Mainz, spent formative years in Paris (1672-6) where he encountered Cartesianism, Malebranche, Arnauld, and Spinoza (whom he visited in 1676), and independently invented the infinitesimal calculus, leading to a bitter priority dispute with Newton. He spent most of his career in the service of the House of Hanover, dying neglected after being passed over when George I became King of England.
philosophical_problems: What is the nature of substance, and how many substances are there?
How can mind and matter, or any two substances, interact, if at all?
Can God's existence be proved by reason alone, and if so, how?
How can the existence of evil be reconciled with a good and omnipotent God who freely chose to create this particular world?
What is the logical relationship between subject and predicate, and what does it imply about the nature of individual substances?

philosophers_discussed.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Primary subject; his life, his popular and esoteric philosophies, his monadology, his proofs of God, his theodicy, and his logic-based metaphysics are all examined.

philosophers_discussed.name: Rene Descartes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented as sharing with Leibniz a philosophy grounded in the notion of substance, though Leibniz differs radically on the number of substances and the nature of matter; Leibniz was influenced by Cartesianism in Paris.

philosophers_discussed.name: Baruch Spinoza
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Leibniz visited him in 1676, discussed philosophy with him for a month, and obtained part of the Ethics in manuscript, but later downplayed the relationship; Leibniz's esoteric system is described as 'largely Spinozistic.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Saint Anselm
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Credited as the inventor of the ontological argument for God's existence, later revived by Descartes and restated more rigorously by Leibniz.

philosophers_discussed.name: Immanuel Kant
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Mentioned as the philosopher who countered the ontological argument (existence is not a predicate) and who pointed out that the cosmological argument secretly depends on the ontological argument.

philosophers_discussed.name: Antoine Arnauld
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Leibniz's correspondent, whose horrified reaction to Leibniz's deterministic esoteric doctrine led Leibniz to keep it secret for the rest of his life.

core_concepts.name: Monads
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Leibniz believed the universe is made up of an infinite number of simple, non-physical, soul-like units called monads, rather than physical matter; even what looks like solid matter is really a colony of these mind-like units.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Simple, unextended substances, each essentially a soul with perceptions of varying clarity, that make up all of reality; Leibniz denied that extension could be an attribute of a true substance because extension implies plurality, so genuine substances must be unextended and therefore mental.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is Leibniz's solution to the problem of substance: rather than three substances (Descartes) or one (Spinoza), he posits infinitely many, each a distinct point of view on the universe.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in the Monadology and the Principles of Nature and of Grace, written for royal patrons.
examples: A human body is composed entirely of monads, each a soul, with one 'dominant monad' constituting what we call the person's mind.
No two monads are exactly alike (the principle of the identity of indiscernibles).
objections: Russell says the doctrine that monads are 'windowless' creates the puzzle of how any monad could know there are others at all - what looks like mirroring the universe could simply be a private dream.
Leibniz is 'guilty of a special inconsistency' in combining subject-predicate logic (which implies monism) with a pluralism of many monads.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell says Leibniz's two kinds of space - subjective (within each monad's perception) and objective (the arrangement of viewpoints) - remain useful for relating perception to physics.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: The 'dominant monad' explains, for Leibniz, what common sense calls the will's control over the body.

core_concepts.name: Windowless monads and pre-established harmony
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Monads cannot causally affect one another at all - they are 'windowless.' What looks like interaction (for example, my will moving my arm) is really the result of God having set up all monads in advance, like an infinite number of perfectly synchronized clocks, so their changes match up without any real causal connection.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that no monad can have any causal relation to any other; each simply unfolds according to its own nature, and the appearance of interaction across monads is explained by a harmony pre-established by God at creation.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It resolves the problem, inherited from Cartesian occasionalism, of how substances that cannot interact can nonetheless appear to affect one another (as in perception or in physical impact).
core_concepts.historical_origin: An extension of the Cartesian 'two clocks' analogy for mind-body correspondence, generalized by Leibniz to an infinite number of monads.
examples: Leibniz compared monads to an infinite number of clocks all arranged by the Creator to strike at the same instant, not because they affect each other but because each is a perfectly accurate mechanism.
objections: If monads never interact, Russell asks how one could know that any others exist at all; the appearance of mirroring the universe might simply be a shared, coincidental 'dream.'
competing_positions: Cartesian occasionalism, in which God intervenes on each occasion rather than pre-arranging everything in advance
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Leibniz argued the pre-established harmony itself was evidence for God's existence, forming his fourth argument for God, generalizable into the argument from design.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Used by Leibniz as a proof of God's existence and providence.

core_concepts.name: The four arguments for God's existence
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Leibniz gave the classic, most polished versions of four traditional proofs that God exists: the ontological argument (from the very definition of a perfect being), the cosmological argument (from the need for a 'sufficient reason' for the universe), the argument from eternal truths (truths like mathematics must exist in an eternal mind), and the argument from pre-established harmony/design.
core_concepts.precise_definition: (1) Ontological: since existence is a 'perfection,' and God is defined as possessing all perfections, God's essence entails His existence. (2) Cosmological: every contingent thing, and the universe as a whole, needs a 'sufficient reason' outside itself, which must be God. (3) From eternal truths: necessary truths (like mathematics) must exist as thoughts in an eternal mind. (4) From pre-established harmony/design: the harmonious coordination of monads (or, more generally, apparent design in nature) points to a beneficent creator.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats Leibniz as the philosopher who 'brought into their final form' these classical proofs, making him the ideal figure through which to examine and critique them, even though modern theologians no longer rely on them.
core_concepts.historical_origin: The ontological argument originates with Saint Anselm and was revived by Descartes; the cosmological argument descends from Aristotle's argument of the unmoved mover; Leibniz restates and refines all four with unusual logical rigor.
examples: Leibniz's written proof, shown to Spinoza, that the concept of God (as the subject of all compatible perfections) is possible, from which existence is then said to follow since existence is itself a perfection.
objections: Kant countered the ontological argument by denying that 'existence' is a predicate; Russell adds that his own theory of descriptions supplies another refutation.
Kant showed the cosmological argument secretly depends on the ontological argument.
The argument from eternal truths is open to the objection that a truth can hardly be said to 'exist' in a mind that merely apprehends it.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes that, despite Kant's supposed demolition of these arguments, metaphysical proofs of God persisted in Hegel, Lotze, and Bradley.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Leibniz's theological optimism, based partly on these proofs, was set out in the Theodicee, written for Queen Charlotte of Prussia.

core_concepts.name: Best of all possible worlds / theodicy
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Leibniz argued that before creating anything, God considered infinitely many possible worlds and chose to create the one with the greatest excess of good over evil - so even though our world contains evil, it is nonetheless the best world logically possible, because some goods (like free will) cannot exist without the risk of some evils (like sin).
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that a possible world is one not contradicting the laws of logic; God, being good, necessarily creates the possible world with the greatest surplus of good over evil, so the evils that exist are logically necessary for a greater compensating good and provide no argument against God's goodness.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It was Leibniz's popular solution to the problem of evil, satisfying enough to please royal patrons like the Queen of Prussia, but Russell judges it 'logically possible, but not very convincing.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out in the Theodicee and the Monadology; famously satirized by Voltaire as the philosophy of Dr. Pangloss, and mocked by F. H. Bradley's remark that 'everything in it is a necessary evil.'
examples: Free will is a great good, but it was logically impossible for God to grant free will while also decreeing there would be no sin, so God permitted Adam's fall as the price of a world with free will.
The comparison of a drink of cold water being more pleasurable after enduring thirst.
objections: Russell constructs a deliberately fantastic mirror-image argument (a Manichaean claim that this is the worst of all possible worlds) to show Leibniz's argument is no more rigorous than its opposite.
Russell notes the argument conveniently comforted the Queen of Prussia while her serfs continued to suffer real evil.
competing_positions: A Manichaean view that the world is designed by a wicked demiurge to maximize suffering, given as a parallel fantastic argument by Russell
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Voltaire's Doctor Pangloss in Candide is a direct satire of Leibniz's popular optimism.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Written to reassure a queen; Russell notes it functioned to justify the comfort of the powerful amid the suffering of their subjects.

core_concepts.name: The esoteric doctrine: subject-predicate logic and the complete concept of substance
core_concepts.plain_explanation: In private, unpublished writings, Leibniz held that every true statement about a thing is really 'built into' the complete concept of that thing from eternity - so everything that will ever happen to you is already part of the very notion of who you are, known fully only to God. This makes Leibniz's private system just as deterministic as Spinoza's, which is why he kept it hidden.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that in every true proposition the predicate is contained in the subject; applied to individual substances, this means the complete 'notion' of an individual (e.g., Alexander the Great, or Adam) already logically contains every predicate that will ever truly be asserted of him, including all future events, though only God's infinite understanding can actually analyze this out.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It reveals what Russell considers the profound, logically serious Leibniz, hidden behind the popular philosopher of free will and possible worlds; it grounds the windowless-monad doctrine (since nothing needs to 'come in' from outside if everything is already contained in the subject's own notion).
core_concepts.historical_origin: Found in Leibniz's letters to Arnauld and in manuscripts first published by Louis Couturat in 1901-3, nearly two centuries after Leibniz's death.
examples: Leibniz's example of Alexander the Great: God, seeing the complete individual notion of Alexander, sees within it whether he would conquer Darius and Porus and even how he would die.
Leibniz's concept of 'compossibility': not all possible things can coexist, and what exists is the largest group of mutually 'compossible' things.
objections: Arnauld reacted with horror, saying the doctrine that a person's individual notion 'involves once for all everything that will ever happen to him' is incompatible with the Christian doctrine of sin and free will.

Russell argues the whole subject-predicate logic underlying it either ignores relations or produces fallacious arguments against their reality, and that a consistent believer in this logic 'should be a monist, like Spinoza' rather than a pluralist.
competing_positions: Leibniz's own published doctrine that human free will 'inclines without necessitating'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell states he was 'the first to notice the importance' of Leibniz's letters to Arnauld for understanding this esoteric doctrine.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Suppressed by Leibniz specifically because it was incompatible with Christian teaching on sin and free will.

core_concepts.name: Characteristica Universalis
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Leibniz dreamed of inventing a kind of universal symbolic logic that would let people resolve any dispute, even in philosophy or morals, simply by calculating - 'Let us calculate' instead of arguing.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A hoped-for generalized symbolic calculus that would reduce reasoning in metaphysics and morals to the same kind of rigor as geometry and algebra, allowing disputes to be settled by calculation rather than disputation.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It reflects Leibniz's foundational belief in the power of logic, and anticipates, however imperfectly, the later development of mathematical logic.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Leibniz's own aspiration, described in his unpublished logical writings.
examples: Leibniz's quoted wish that philosophers with disputes might simply 'take their pencils in their hands, sit down to their slates,' and calculate.
objections: Leibniz abstained from publishing his mathematical logic because he kept finding what he believed must be errors in Aristotle's theory of the syllogism, which out of respect for Aristotle he assumed must be his own mistakes.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell says that had Leibniz published this work, he would have been the founder of mathematical logic a century and a half before it actually emerged.

arguments.title: The ontological argument (Leibniz's version)
premises: God is defined as the subject of all perfections.
A perfection is a simple, positive, unlimited quality.
No two perfections, so defined, can be incompatible with each other.
Existence is itself one of the perfections.
arguments.conclusion: There is, or can be conceived, a most perfect Being, and it follows that He exists, since existence is among the perfections.
arguments.explanation: Leibniz supplements Anselm's and Descartes's version by first proving that the concept of God (as subject of all compatible perfections) is coherent/possible, and only then concludes that such a being must exist because existence is itself a perfection it must possess.
objections: Kant's objection that 'existence' is not a predicate.
Russell notes his own theory of descriptions offers another kind of refutation.
Russell says it is easier to feel the argument must be fallacious than to pinpoint exactly where the fallacy lies.
implications: If sound, would establish God's existence through reason alone, independent of experience.

arguments.title: The cosmological argument
premises: Every particular thing in the world is 'contingent' - it would be logically possible for it not to exist.
This is true of the whole universe, even if the universe has always existed.
Everything must have a sufficient reason for its existence.
The universe as a whole must therefore have a sufficient reason, which cannot lie within the universe itself.
arguments.conclusion: There must be a sufficient reason for the universe outside the universe, and this is God.
arguments.explanation: Unlike the simpler First-Cause argument (which wrongly assumes every series must have a first term), Leibniz's version does not depend on the universe having had a beginning in time; it depends entirely on accepting the principle of sufficient reason.
objections: If the principle of sufficient reason is denied, the argument collapses.
Kant showed that this argument secretly depends on the ontological argument, since a 'necessary Being' is precisely one whose essence involves existence.
implications: Its apparent greater plausibility compared to the ontological argument is, Russell says, deceptive, since the two are ultimately linked.

arguments.title: The argument from the eternal truths
premises: Some truths (like mathematical truths) are always true, unlike contingent truths (like 'it is raining').
Truths are part of the contents of minds.
The ultimate reason for contingent truths must be found in necessary, eternal truths.
A reason for what exists must itself, in some sense, exist.
arguments.conclusion: Eternal truths must exist as thoughts in the mind of God.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as essentially another form of the cosmological argument, tracing a similar (less developed) argument back to Plato's deduction of immortality from the eternity of the ideas.
objections: It is open to the objection that a truth can hardly be said to 'exist' in a mind which merely apprehends it.

arguments.title: The argument from pre-established harmony (generalizable to the argument from design)
premises: Yet their perceptions correspond as if they did interact, like clocks all keeping perfect time.
Such coordination without interaction requires a single external cause that set them all in harmony.
arguments.conclusion: There must be an outside Cause (God) that established this harmony.
arguments.explanation: In its strict form the argument depends on accepting Leibniz's monadology; but Russell notes it can be generalized, freed of the monad theory, into the broader argument from design - that features of the world are better explained by a beneficent purpose than by blind natural forces.
objections: The difficulty besetting the whole monadology: if monads never interact, how could any one of them know there are others, rather than merely dreaming that there are?
implications: The generalized design argument, unlike the other three, could in principle prove only a limited God (not necessarily omnipotent or omniscient), since it argues from the empirically observed character of the world rather than from pure logic.

arguments.title: The best-of-all-possible-worlds argument (theodicy)
premises: God, before creation, contemplated infinitely many logically possible worlds.
Being good, God chose to create the one with the greatest excess of good over evil.
Some great goods (e.g., free will) are logically inseparable from certain evils (e.g., sin).
arguments.conclusion: The actual world, despite containing evil, is the best of all possible worlds, and its evil affords no argument against God's goodness.
arguments.explanation: God foresaw Adam would sin but still created a world with free will because a world with free will and some sin has a greater surplus of good over evil than a world without free will at all.
objections: Russell constructs a parallel Manichaean argument (that this could equally be called the worst of all possible worlds) to show the reasoning is not uniquely compelling.
Russell states plainly that the argument is 'logically possible, but not very convincing.'
implications: This popular doctrine, aimed at reassuring the powerful, is sharply distinguished by Russell from Leibniz's much more rigorous, privately-held deterministic system.

key_distinctions: The 'popular' Leibniz (published, optimistic, aimed at princes) vs. the 'esoteric' Leibniz (unpublished, deterministic, logically rigorous)
Windowless monads (no causal interaction) vs. apparent interaction via pre-established harmony
Analytic propositions (predicate contained in subject) as the basis of both the law of contradiction and, in the esoteric doctrine, the law of sufficient reason
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Leibniz's metaphysics of substance follows Descartes and Spinoza in starting from the logical category of subject and predicate; his ontological argument descends from Saint Anselm (via Descartes); his cosmological argument descends from Aristotle's unmoved mover; his esoteric philosophy is described by Russell as 'largely Spinozistic' and as belonging to the same logic-driven tradition running from Parmenides through Plato.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Leibniz's disciple Wolf dominated German universities (making German philosophy 'pedantic and arid') until Kant's Critique of Pure Reason; his metaphysical proofs of God persisted, in modified form, in Hegel, Lotze, and Bradley, despite Kant's supposed refutation of them.
political_social_context: Leibniz spent his career serving the Archbishop of Mainz and then the House of Hanover, writing his popular optimistic philosophy for royal patrons (Prince Eugene of Savoy, Queen Charlotte of Prussia); Russell notes drily that his theodicy conveniently satisfied a queen whose serfs continued to suffer real evils.
religion_science_culture_context: Leibniz independently invented the infinitesimal calculus (1675-6), leading to a bitter and discreditable priority dispute with Newton that damaged his standing in England; his interest in reuniting the Christian Churches was one of several projects (along with a history of the House of Brunswick) that occupied his later career.
russell_presentation: Russell portrays Leibniz as a towering intellect but a morally unimpressive figure, contrasting him sharply and repeatedly with Spinoza's integrity. He divides Leibniz's philosophy into a shallow, published system designed to please patrons - centered on monads, the best of all possible worlds, and metaphysical proofs of God - and a profound, unpublished, largely Spinozistic system that Leibniz suppressed after Arnauld's horrified reaction convinced him it was too shocking to publish. Russell walks through the classic proofs of God's existence in their most rigorous, Leibnizian form (ontological, cosmological, from eternal truths, and from design), presenting careful, largely Kantian objections to each. He treats the doctrine of the best of all possible worlds as clever but unconvincing, mocking it with a deliberately parallel 'worst of all possible worlds' argument. Finally, Russell gives real credit to the 'esoteric' Leibniz, presenting the subject-predicate logic underlying the complete-concept theory of substance as intellectually serious even though ultimately mistaken, and faults Leibniz for inconsistently combining a logic that implies monism with a metaphysics of plural, independent monads. Russell closes by praising Leibniz's genuine achievements: his invention of the calculus, his pioneering (if unpublished) work in mathematical logic, and the continuing usefulness of his distinction between subjective and objective space.
key_takeaways: Russell distinguishes a 'popular' Leibniz, who wrote to please royal patrons, from a more profound 'esoteric' Leibniz whose deterministic, Spinozistic views were kept hidden and only published from manuscript nearly two centuries after his death.

Leibniz's monads are simple, unextended, mind-like substances that make up all reality; they are 'windowless' and never causally interact, appearing to correspond only through God's pre-established harmony.

Leibniz gave the most rigorous classical versions of four arguments for God's existence: ontological, cosmological, from eternal truths, and from design/pre-established harmony - all of which Russell subjects to detailed critique.

His theodicy holds that God freely chose to create the best of all logically possible worlds, in which some evils (like sin) are the unavoidable price of great goods (like free will); Russell finds this clever but unpersuasive.

In private writings, Leibniz held that the complete 'notion' of any individual substance already contains every predicate true of it for all time, a doctrine as deterministic as Spinoza's and one Leibniz suppressed after Arnauld's objections.
Russell credits Leibniz with genuine achievements: co-inventing the infinitesimal calculus and doing pioneering, unpublished work in mathematical logic.
study_notes:
The organizing idea of this chapter is Russell's split between the 'two Leibnizes.' Keep asking, for any doctrine presented, which Leibniz is speaking: the one performing for Queen Charlotte and Prince Eugene, or the one confiding in private manuscripts and in his letters to Arnauld. The popular doctrines (monads, pre-established harmony, best of all possible worlds) are individually clever and often ingenious, but Russell treats them as somewhat theatrical - designed to reassure rather than to follow the argument wherever it leads. The esoteric doctrine, by contrast, is the one Russell takes most seriously as philosophy, even though he ultimately rejects it: it is the purest example in the chapter of deducing sweeping metaphysical conclusions from a single logical premise (that in every true proposition, the predicate is contained in the subject).

It is worth carefully separating the four arguments for God's existence, since they are easy to blur together. The ontological argument tries to get existence out of a definition alone, with no appeal to experience at all. The cosmological argument starts from the fact that the world exists and asks for a 'sufficient reason.' The argument from eternal truths starts from truths like mathematics and asks where they could 'live' if not in an eternal mind. The argument from design (the loosened version of pre-established harmony) is the only one of the four that is genuinely empirical - it looks at features of the actual world and infers a purposeful cause. Russell's key move, following Kant, is to show that the cosmological and eternal-truths arguments both secretly smuggle in the ontological argument, so that if the ontological argument fails, so do they, leaving only the empirical design argument standing (and even that, Russell notes, could at most prove a limited, not necessarily omnipotent, designer).

Finally, notice the recurring theme of inconsistency: Russell repeatedly flags places where Leibniz's logic points one way (toward Spinoza-style monism) while his conclusions go another way (toward a plurality of monads), and suggests this inconsistency, much like the inconsistency Russell later finds productive in Descartes, is part of what makes Leibniz's system so fertile even though it cannot be fully defended as self-consistent.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: One of the countless simple, soul-like units Leibniz believed everything in the universe is really made of.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A simple, unextended substance that perceives the universe from its own point of view with varying clarity; monads are 'windowless' and do not causally interact.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: God's advance arrangement that makes all the separate, non-interacting monads appear to affect each other, like clocks set in advance to strike together.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Leibniz's doctrine that apparent causal interaction between substances is really the result of each substance's independent, God-ordained unfolding matching every other's.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that nothing happens without some reason or explanation for why it is so and not otherwise.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Leibniz's principle that every true proposition has a reason why it is true; in his published works, applied to contingent truths as motivating rather than logically necessitating; in his esoteric doctrine, held to mean that every true proposition is ultimately analytic.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A statement that is true just because of what its words mean, like 'all bachelors are unmarried.'
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Leibniz, a proposition in which the predicate is contained in the notion of the subject; the basis of both the law of contradiction and, in his esoteric philosophy, the law of sufficient reason.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Able to exist together at the same time without contradiction.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Leibniz's term for possible entities that can coexist without logical contradiction; the actual world is, in his esoteric writings, the largest group of compossible entities.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The argument that God must exist just because of how 'perfect being' is defined.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The argument, from Anselm through Descartes to Leibniz, that a most perfect being's essence entails its existence, since existence is itself a perfection.

questions.prompt: What does Russell mean by describing Leibniz's philosophy as 'two systems'?
questions.answer: One system is the popular philosophy Leibniz published to please princes and princesses - optimistic, orthodox, and centered on the doctrine of the best of all possible worlds; the other is a profound, largely Spinozistic and rigorously logical system found in his unpublished manuscripts, kept secret after his correspondent Arnauld reacted with horror to its deterministic implications.
questions.explanation: This distinction structures the whole chapter and explains why Leibniz can seem shallow in his published Monadology yet be a 'supreme intellect' underneath.

questions.prompt: Why does Leibniz call monads 'windowless,' and what problem does this create?
questions.answer: Monads cannot causally affect or be affected by one another at all - nothing 'comes in' or 'goes out.' This creates the problem of explaining apparent interaction (as in perception, or physical impact), which Leibniz solves by positing a pre-established harmony arranged by God rather than genuine causal exchange.
questions.explanation: Russell notes this raises the further problem of how a monad could ever know other monads exist, since it never actually interacts with them.

questions.prompt: Compare Leibniz's cosmological argument for God's existence with the simpler 'First-Cause' argument, according to Russell.
questions.answer: The simple First-Cause argument assumes every causal series must have a first term, which Russell notes is false (e.g., the series of proper fractions has no first term). Leibniz's version avoids this flaw: it does not depend on the universe having a beginning in time, but instead argues that the universe as a whole, even if eternal, is 'contingent' and needs a sufficient reason outside itself. However, Kant showed that this stronger version secretly depends on the ontological argument.
questions.explanation: This distinction shows why Russell treats Leibniz's version as more sophisticated, even though it ultimately faces the same underlying difficulty.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher's horrified reaction to Leibniz's private doctrine (that an individual's complete notion contains everything that will ever happen to them) led Leibniz to keep the doctrine secret?
questions.explanation: Arnauld wrote that he found 'so many things which alarm me' in Leibniz's letters that he doubted anyone would accept them, prompting Leibniz's lifelong policy of secrecy about his real views.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Leibniz's argument for the doctrine that the actual world is the best of all possible worlds, and state Russell's main objection to it.
questions.answer: God contemplated infinitely many logically possible worlds before creation; being good, He chose to create the one with the greatest surplus of good over evil; some great goods (like free will) cannot exist without certain corresponding evils (like sin), so a world with free will and some sin is better than one with neither. Russell objects that this reasoning is not uniquely compelling, since one could construct an equally 'logical' opposite argument (a Manichaean claim that this is the worst of all possible worlds), showing the doctrine is 'logically possible, but not very convincing.'
questions.explanation: Russell deliberately constructs the parody argument to expose the weakness of Leibniz's theodicy.

questions.prompt: What genuine, lasting achievements does Russell credit to Leibniz, apart from his metaphysics?
questions.answer: Russell credits Leibniz with independently inventing the infinitesimal calculus, being a pioneer of mathematical logic (whose unpublished work, had it appeared, would have advanced the field by a century and a half), and originating a distinction between subjective and objective space that Russell finds still useful for relating perception to physics.
questions.explanation: This is part of Russell's concluding, more sympathetic assessment of Leibniz's overall importance.

flashcards.back: Simple, unextended, soul-like substances that make up all of reality; each perceives the universe from its own point of view with varying degrees of clarity.
Because they cannot causally interact with each other at all - nothing passes between them; apparent interaction is explained instead by pre-established harmony.

God's advance arrangement causing the independent unfolding of all monads to correspond, producing the appearance of interaction without any actual causal connection - like an infinite set of clocks all set to strike together.

flashcards.front: Name Leibniz's four arguments for God's existence.
flashcards.back: The ontological argument, the cosmological argument, the argument from eternal truths, and the argument from pre-established harmony (generalizable to the argument from design).

flashcards.front: What is Kant's objection to the ontological argument?
flashcards.back: That 'existence' is not a predicate, so you cannot build existence into a thing's definition and then 'discover' that it exists.

flashcards.front: According to Kant, why does the cosmological argument secretly depend on the ontological argument?
flashcards.back: Because it concludes there must be a 'necessary Being,' and a necessary Being is defined as one whose essence involves existence - which is exactly what the ontological argument tries to establish.

flashcards.front: What is Leibniz's doctrine of the 'best of all possible worlds'?
flashcards.back: God, being good, chose to create the possible world with the greatest surplus of good over evil; some great goods (like free will) require the possibility of corresponding evils (like sin).

flashcards.front: Who satirized Leibniz's optimism, and as what character?
flashcards.back: Voltaire, as Doctor Pangloss in Candide.

flashcards.front: What is the 'esoteric' Leibniz, and why was it kept secret?
flashcards.back: A private, unpublished doctrine, discovered mainly in manuscripts published by Couturat in 1901-3, holding that every individual substance's complete concept already contains everything that will ever happen to it - a determinism Leibniz hid after Arnauld reacted with horror.

flashcards.front: What does 'compossible' mean in Leibniz's private philosophy?
flashcards.back: Able to coexist without logical contradiction; the actual world, on this view, is the largest possible group of mutually compossible things.
His dream of a universal symbolic calculus that would let philosophical and moral disputes be settled by calculation rather than argument.

flashcards.front: What real, lasting contribution did Leibniz make to mathematics?
flashcards.back: He independently invented the infinitesimal calculus (1675-6), leading to a bitter priority dispute with Newton.

flashcards.front: What inconsistency does Russell find between Leibniz's logic and his metaphysics of monads?
flashcards.back: Leibniz's subject-predicate logic implies that a consistent thinker should be a monist (like Spinoza), yet Leibniz asserts a plurality of many monads, which is inconsistent with that logic.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, why did Leibniz maintain two distinct philosophical systems?
options: He changed his mind completely partway through his life
His published system was designed to please princes and princesses, while his real, more profound views were kept private
He was forced by the Church to hide his true beliefs
He wanted separate systems for mathematics and for ethics
quiz.explanation: Russell explains that what Leibniz published was designed to win royal approbation, while his best, more profound thought remained unpublished in his desk.

quiz.prompt: What does Leibniz mean by calling monads 'windowless'?
options: They have no way to perceive light
They cannot causally interact with one another at all
They exist only inside physical bodies
They can only be perceived by God
quiz.explanation: No monad can affect or be affected by any other monad; apparent interaction is explained by pre-established harmony instead.

quiz.prompt: Which philosopher is credited with inventing the ontological argument, later revived by Descartes and refined by Leibniz?
options: Aristotle
Saint Anselm
Thomas Aquinas
Plato
quiz.explanation: Russell states the ontological argument 'was invented by Saint Anselm,' though rejected by Saint Thomas and later revived by Descartes.

quiz.prompt: What is Kant's specific objection to the ontological argument, as Russell reports it?
options: That God cannot be defined at all
That 'existence' is not a predicate
That perfection is a meaningless concept
That the argument commits a category mistake about time
quiz.explanation: Russell reports Kant's counter that existence is not a predicate, so it cannot simply be included among a being's defining perfections.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, Leibniz's cosmological argument requires that the universe had an actual beginning in time.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly notes that, unlike the simple First-Cause argument, Leibniz's cosmological argument does not depend on the universe having had a beginning in time.

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's chief criticism of Leibniz's doctrine of the best of all possible worlds?
options: That it is logically inconsistent on its own terms
That an equally 'logical' opposite (a worst-of-all-possible-worlds argument) could be constructed just as easily, showing the reasoning is not uniquely compelling
That Leibniz never actually wrote it down
That it was later disproved by Newtonian physics
quiz.explanation: Russell constructs a parody Manichaean argument to show that Leibniz's theodicy is 'logically possible, but not very convincing.'

quiz.prompt: In Leibniz's esoteric philosophy, what does it mean to say the complete 'notion' of Alexander the Great includes all his predicates?
options: Only his physical description is included
Every true fact about him, past, present, and future, is logically contained in the very concept of Alexander, knowable fully only by God
It means only his royal title is essential to him
It applies only to necessary truths, not contingent facts
quiz.explanation: Russell quotes Leibniz's own example that God, seeing Alexander's individual notion, sees within it even whether he would conquer Darius and Porus and how he would die.

quiz.prompt: Leibniz's dreamed-of universal symbolic calculus, meant to let disputes be settled by calculation rather than argument, was called the ________.
options: Monadology
Characteristica Universalis
Theodicee
Principia Logica
quiz.explanation: Russell describes Leibniz's hope for a 'Characteristica Universalis' by which thinking could be replaced by calculation.

essay_prompts.prompt: Russell argues that Leibniz's four proofs of God's existence are all vulnerable to a single underlying weakness once the ontological argument is rejected. Reconstruct all four arguments and evaluate whether Russell is right that the cosmological and eternal-truths arguments both secretly depend on the ontological argument, while the design argument alone remains independently empirical.
rubric: Correctly explains the dependency relationships Russell identifies
Original evaluation of whether the design argument really escapes the criticism

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare the 'popular' Leibniz of the Monadology and Theodicee with the 'esoteric' Leibniz of the letters to Arnauld. Which one does Russell consider more philosophically serious, and do you agree with his assessment? Support your answer with specific doctrines from the chapter.
rubric: Explains Russell's evaluative preference and his reasons
Historical accuracy regarding Leibniz's biography and publication history
